attribution: Shukla Yajurveda (final part of the Shatapatha Brahmana); author unknown, with much teaching ascribed to the sage Yajnavalkya
period: Generally considered one of the two oldest Upanishads; many scholars place its core around the 7th–6th centuries BCE, with later additions; dating is debated
summary: The longest and probably oldest Upanishad, a collection of dialogues and debates, many featuring Yajnavalkya, on the Self, Brahman, death and rebirth.
whyRead: Much of what later Indian philosophy argues about is first stated here: the identity of Self and Brahman, the Self as the unseen seer, the 'not this, not this' method, and an early account of karma and rebirth. It is long and demanding, but its dialogues, especially between Yajnavalkya and his wife Maitreyi, are vivid.
story: King Janaka of Videha hosts a debate and offers a prize of cows to the most learned; Yajnavalkya claims it and is questioned by a series of challengers, including the woman philosopher Gargi. Elsewhere, as he prepares to leave home for the renunciant life, Yajnavalkya teaches his wife Maitreyi, who asks whether wealth could make her immortal, that everything is dear for the sake of the Self.
questions: What happens to a person at death?

keyTeachings.title: I am Brahman
keyTeachings.text: The text declares that whoever knows 'I am Brahman' becomes all this, one of the classical mahavakyas.

keyTeachings.title: Not this, not this
keyTeachings.text: Brahman or the Self is described as 'neti neti', not this, not this: no positive description captures it. This became a key method in Advaita.

keyTeachings.title: Dear for the sake of the Self
keyTeachings.text: Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi that husband, wife, wealth and all things are dear not for their own sake but for the sake of the Self, which is to be seen, heard, reflected and meditated upon.

keyTeachings.title: The unseen seer
keyTeachings.text: The Self is the seer of seeing that cannot itself be seen, the knower that cannot be known as an object.

keyTeachings.title: As one acts, so one becomes
keyTeachings.text: An early formulation of karma links a person's desires, will and actions to their future state and rebirth.

keyTeachings.title: The inner controller
keyTeachings.text: Yajnavalkya describes the Self as the inner controller (antaryamin) dwelling within all things, which they do not know. Ramanuja makes this passage central.

structure.label: 6 chapters (adhyayas) in 3 sections (kandas)
structure.note: Traditionally the Madhu, Yajnavalkya (Muni) and Khila kandas

structure.label: Two recensions
structure.note: Kanva and Madhyandina, with differences in numbering
